Campaign Editor · Shell & Lifecycle · Wireframe Set

The editor, end to end, at every display it will meet

The campaign editor has exactly one responsive state and one hard floor — 1920 × 880 effective pixels. This set draws its whole lifecycle at that floor, draws each of its seven workspaces, and then shows what the shell does with the room an FHD, QHD or 4K display actually gives it. The frames are real CSS layout at true effective pixels, so every number quoted in a caption was measured after mount, not estimated.

Drawn against CEUI-1/3/4/5/7/8, CEUI-S1–S12 Register campaign_editor_ui_open_questions_2026-08-12.md Tracker DISCUSS-CAMPAIGN-EDITOR-UI-2026-07-31 Date 2026-08-14
READ FIRST

What is settled here and what is not

The shell is drawn as ruled. The interiors are drawn as frames. Section A of the CEUI register closed on 2026-08-14, which fixes the composition, the tab model, the fixed docks, the header contents, the seven workspaces and the floor. Sections B–F are still open — CEUI-9–12, 17–21, 23–31, 33–36, 39, 40 — and so are the twelve NMTE residues scheduled as S11. Anywhere this set shows a dashed red outline, the region's position and role are ruled and its interior is not. Do not read a dashed region as a design proposal.

The gate has lifted — updated 2026-08-15. When this set was drawn the CEUI walk was still open and the shell was drawn ahead of the gate by owner decision. The walk closed on 2026-08-14 ([CEUI-S1]–[CEUI-S50]), and [DSX-S29] then made a UBS gate turn on its album being approved rather than on its walk closing. The owner approved this album on 2026-08-15, so UBS-8 is closed — the first gate released under that standard — and this set is the editor's authoritative reference. The UUI-15 album hold now waits on UBS-6's approval and UBS-7's walk.

New questions are raised, not answered. Nothing about the editor's behaviour above its floor has ever been ruled. Section 7 collects ten findings this pass produced, each with options and a recommendation, for an owner walk. They are marked proposed throughout.

SHEET 1

The display model

CEUI-5 · CEUI-S1 · CEUI-S2 ratified

Three ratified pieces combine into one arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what makes "FHD, UHD and 4K" a tractable question rather than an open-ended one.

  • [CEUI-5] — the floor is 1920 × 880, a maximized browser window on the most common desktop display, with a ~200 px allowance for tab strip, omnibox, bookmarks bar and taskbar. Below the floor the editor shows an explanatory minimum-size state; it never degrades into a compromised layout.
  • [CEUI-S1] — the player's Menu Scale does not reach the editor. The editor owns its own scale knob, built as a fourth token column through the same assembler.
  • [CEUI-S2] — the floor is tested against window ÷ editor scale, not raw window pixels. Effective pixels are the unit of this whole document.

The two factors multiply, and only one of them is ours

The OS/browser scale factor sets how many physical pixels a CSS pixel spends. The editor scale sets how many CSS pixels an effective pixel spends. The product is what the author's eye actually receives.

effective = windowcss ÷ s  ·  physical-per-effective = DPR × s

Combining the two gives the result that governs this sheet. Hold physical-per-effective ≥ 1.0 — never render editor type physically smaller than an FHD display at 100% shows it — and the reachable effective viewport collapses to a single expression:

max effective viewport = physical resolution − (chrome allowance × DPR)

So the display's physical resolution — not its CSS window, not its OS scale setting — is the real ceiling on how much editor an author can have. Two displays that report identical CSS windows are not equivalent: the 4K one can trade its scale knob for room and the FHD one cannot. That is the entire FHD-versus-4K story, and it is why this set has exactly three width columns rather than a continuum.

Three results worth stating plainly. (1) A 4K display at Windows' default 200% scaling produces exactly the floor window — the same 1920×880 an FHD display gives at 100%. The floor was derived from FHD and 4K lands on it by coincidence of arithmetic. (2) 4K at 150% and QHD at 100% are the same window, so the whole FHD/QHD/4K range reduces to three distinct effective viewports. (3) The only row that fails outright is FHD at 125% — a common Windows default on 1080p laptops — and it fails on height, by 216 px, not on width.

SHEET 2

Reading a frame

Heavy outer stroke — the editor window, in effective px
Chrome fill — header, workspace bar, status bar
Dock fill — tree, Inspector, bottom panel
Plain fill — the document area
Diagonal hatch — a canvas — map, graph, game view
Dashed red outline — position ruled, interior NOT ruled
Amber fill — the selected row or active chip
Violet fill — the embedded session — pack-themed, not editor-themed

Label text inside frames is set at 16–18 effective px so it survives the 0.55× reduction. That is an annotation size, not the editor's type size — real editor body type is 14 effective px and is drawn as grey bars. Where a measurement matters it is reported numerically in the caption rather than trusted to the eye.

SHEET 4

The lifecycle, eleven states

CEUI-S3 · S4 · S5 · S6 · S8 · S9 · S10 · S13

Every frame is 1920 × 880 effective — the floor, and the state in which the editor must be proven. The editor takes a copy, the author works in staged transactions, tests inside an embedded session, and leaves only by an explicit export. There is no implicit write-back anywhere on this path.

There is no entry transition, by [CEUI-S13]. The editor is reachable only from the main menu, where no pack is active, so it never has to end a run and never shows a confirmation to do so. An earlier draft of this sheet opened with that dialog; it was drawn from [CEUI-S9] call 2's quit-to-shell framing, which described a transition the entry point makes impossible. The substance of call 2 survives and is stronger for it — the editor still requires no active campaign, as a precondition rather than as something the editor performs. A player mid-campaign quits to the menu through the shell's own existing confirmation, and the editor adds no second one.

That precondition is ratified and unbuilt — see EW-10. [CSA-28] clause (f) ruled that quit-to-shell deactivates, but DataManager.deactivate_campaign_package() has no production caller and MainMenu.gd reads only the installed-pack registry. Today the main menu is reached with content still loaded. Nothing depends on that yet; the editor would be the first thing that does.

L1 · Editor home — no document open

Three entry actions, one model. [CEUI-S9]'s strict separation means every one of them produces a copy; none of them opens an installed pack in place.

CEUI-S9 · CEUI-39 · CEUI-S4

L2 · Import a copy from the library

The editor imports a copy and the library original is never touched. This is what makes CL-ADV-01's installed packs are immutable structurally true instead of a policy the editor has to remember.

CEUI-S9

L3 · Working — a staged transaction per tab

The ordinary document model: open, change, save; an interruption reverts. Each tab is its own transaction with its own dirty state, and history is session-scoped.

CEUI-3 · CEUI-S6

L4 · Raw JSON, as a peer view

A plain text view of one record, revalidating on commit. Not read-only, and not a tab inside the form — it is the fallback for when the structured editor fails on a record, so it cannot live inside the thing that broke.

CEUI-S5 · CEUI-22

L5 · Renaming an id touches records you do not have open

Opt-in, confirmed per rename, naming how many records and which. The rewrite cannot be automatically undone, so a recovery snapshot is taken immediately before it commits.

CEUI-S8 · CEUI-36 · CEUI-37

L6 · Validate

The bottom panel is the issue surface. Its position is ruled by CEUI-1; its severity model, grouping and quick-fix behaviour are CEUI-17–20 and unwalked.

CEUI-1 · CEUI-17–20 open

L7 · Test — the embedded playable session

The full runtime playing the pack being edited, inside the editor window. Not a preview surface and not a launch-out.

CEUI-S3 · DLUX-15 · L10N-16

L8 · Test at a Compact preview

The same session at 360 × 640 — how an author checks a phone layout. The editor chrome does not change size class; only the sub-viewport does.

CEUI-S3 · CEUI-5 amendment

L9 · Export — two destinations, one validation gate

Export-to-library (playable, lands through CampaignPackInstaller) and export-to-file (a zip, or a browser download through TransferFileService). They share the gate and differ only in destination.

CEUI-S9 · CEUI-S10 · CEUI-38

L10 · Leaving

The working copy survives the session. Nothing about leaving the editor publishes anything.

CEUI-S9 · CEUI-S6

L11 · Below the floor

1536 × 664 — an FHD display at 125% OS scaling, the one row in Sheet 1 that fails outright.

SHEET 6

FHD → QHD → 4K

width response proposed

Four width responses, one per kind of content

The editor is a single size class, so extra width cannot be answered by a breakpoint. It has to be answered by what the content is. This pass proposes four rules, and every workspace is one of the four.

ResponseRuleWorkspacesAt 3840 effective
Canvas fillsTakes all remaining width and height. More width is more map, more graph, more zoom headroom. Maps, GraphCentre canvas reaches 3180 × 1598 px
Grid reflowsFixed tile size, column count grows with width. Never stretches a tile. Assets8 → 22 columns
Form capsSingle-column forms cap at an 880 px measure and centre. Extra width becomes gutter, then a second document column. Content, ReleaseSplit offered above 2400 px of centre
Table extendsFixed key column, locale columns added until width runs out. Localization4 → 13 locales
Simulator is fixedSized by the simulated size class, not by the editor. Extra editor width becomes device surround. TestGame view unchanged; 1:1 becomes possible

The fifth row is the one most likely to be got wrong in implementation. [CEUI-S3] put a real playable session inside the editor and [CEUI-S2] made the editor's own scale independent of it, which means the embedded game view derives its size class from its sub-viewport. Stretching that view to fill a 4K editor would silently change the size class the author thinks they are previewing — the exact failure [DLUX-15]'s per-size-class preview obligation exists to prevent.

Uniform 0.55×. Wide frames scroll inside their own container.

The workspace that actually wants a 4K display.

SHEET 7

Findings for the owner

ten, none ruled

Each carries options and a recommendation, in the register's format, so they can be walked rather than re-derived. None of them is answered by drawing.

EW-1 Nothing bounds how far the editor scale knob may go down

[CEUI-S2] made the floor effective rather than raw and named the scale knob as the remedy, which rescues the 1366×768 author the original cost paragraph excluded. But the knob has no lower bound. Clearing 880 effective px on a 1366×768 laptop requires 0.64×, at which editor type is 64% of the physical size an FHD display shows at 100% — roughly 9 physical px for 14 px body text.

A — no bound; the author owns the consequence. B — hard-stop the knob at the value where DPR × scale = 1.0, so the editor never renders type physically smaller than FHD@100%. C — allow it, but warn below that line, reusing [UUI-18]'s confirm-or-revert, which [CEUI-S1] already inherited for this exact slider.

Recommendation: C. B silently re-excludes every author [CEUI-S2] just rescued, and on a high-DPR display the same scale value is perfectly legible — a fixed stop cannot tell the two cases apart. The confirm-or-revert dialog can, because it fires on the measured result rather than on the setting.

EW-2 The floor and the ceiling are the same number on FHD, and only on FHD

An FHD display at 100% produces exactly 1920 × 880 and cannot produce more without going below the legibility line. QHD reaches 2560 × 1240 and 4K reaches 3840 × 1960, both at full legibility. So the floor is a working layout for one class of display and a minimum for the others — and every above-floor behaviour in this album is invisible to the FHD author who is, by [CEUI-5]'s own reasoning, the typical one.

A — design only the floor; treat extra width as gutter everywhere. B — design the floor plus proportional growth. C — design the floor plus content-kind responses (Sheet 6).

Recommendation: C, with the consequence stated: every above-floor affordance must be additive, never a relocation. If the split view or a second panel column ever becomes the place a control lives, the FHD author loses that control — and they are the majority case.

EW-3 Three viewports, not a continuum — but only if the chrome allowance holds

The whole FHD/QHD/4K range collapses to three effective viewports because 4K@200% equals FHD@100% and 4K@150% equals QHD@100%. That collapse depends on the 200 CSS px chrome allowance being roughly right. It is a pessimistic estimate — tab strip, omnibox, bookmarks bar and taskbar all present — and a typical browser spends closer to 120.

A — keep 200 as a fixed design constant. B — measure the real window at runtime and test the floor against what is actually there. C — keep 200 for design, measure at runtime for the gate.

Recommendation: C. The design needs a fixed number to draw against; the gate must test the real window, or an author with a 1080p display and a bookmark-bar-free browser gets refused an editor that would have fitted. This is one line of code and it is the difference between the floor being a specification and being a guess.

EW-4 At the floor, the document area is 552 px tall with the bottom panel open

Measured, not estimated: 880 − 44 header − 34 workspace bar − 22 status bar − 28 tab strip − 200 panel = 552, less the form's own padding. That is nineteen rows at the editor pitch, in the workspace where records are actually authored, on the display class the floor was derived from.

A — accept it; the panel is collapsible and the author collapses it. B — default the panel collapsed below a height threshold and open above it. C — shorten the chrome — merge the workspace bar into the header, drop the status bar.

Recommendation: B, which is what this album draws. C is tempting and wrong: [CEUI-S11] ruled the header keeps labels always and scrolls on overflow, so merging seven workspace chips into a header that already holds six actions guarantees the scroll fires at the only viewport the editor has, in every locale.

EW-5 The bottom panel's span and default are unruled, and the workspaces disagree

CEUI-1 ruled a collapsible bottom panel and stopped there. Two things follow that it does not settle: whether the panel spans the centre column only (drawn here) or the full window width beneath both docks, and whether its default state is global or per workspace. The workspaces genuinely want different answers — Release wants it tall and open, Maps wants it collapsed, Content wants it open at 1240 and collapsed at 880.

A — full width, one global default. B — centre column only, one global default. C — centre column only, default per workspace, remembered per workspace.

Recommendation: C. Full width fights the docks for the tree and Inspector's vertical room, which are the two regions with the least of it. A per-workspace default is not personalization — [CEUI-4] ruled layouts fixed for v1 — it is a per-workspace constant, and it costs one value per workspace.

EW-6 A status bar is drawn that no ruling asked for

Four pieces of state need somewhere to live and none of them belongs in CEUI-7's header list: which working copy is active, which installed pack it was copied from, which context owns the keyboard ([CEUI-S3] point 4), and the standing validation count. This album puts them in a 22 px status bar.

A — extend the header. B — a status bar, as drawn. C — distribute them — identity in the header, keyboard owner in the Test toolbar, validation count on the panel tab.

Recommendation: B. A adds to a header that [CEUI-S11] already expects to overflow in translation. C is what the frames would do if the status bar were rejected, and it means the keyboard owner is only visible in the workspace where it is least ambiguous — the arbitration problem exists precisely when focus is somewhere unexpected.

EW-7 The split view above 2400 px is a new affordance built from a ruled primitive

A single 880 px form in a 3180 px centre column leaves 2300 px of gutter. The proposal is a second document column above a 2400 px centre. It invents nothing: [CEUI-3] ruled tabs, and [CEUI-S6] ruled each tab an independent staged transaction, so a split is two tab groups rather than a new document model.

A — no split; gutter is acceptable. B — automatic split above the threshold. C — the split is offered above the threshold and off by default.

Recommendation: C. An automatic split changes the layout an author sees when they resize a window, which is exactly the instability [CEUI-4]'s fixed-layout ruling was protecting against. Offered-and-remembered keeps the ruling intact and still spends the room.

EW-8 Two themes render simultaneously, and the metrics/paint split now has to hold

[CEUI-S3] point 5 noted it; the frames make it concrete. Editor chrome is chrome-themed ([UUI-14]) and the embedded game view is pack-themed ([UUI-16]) in the same window at the same time, drawn violet throughout this set. Settings was already accepted as one boundary-crossing surface, so this is a second instance of a known shape — but it turns [UUI-9]/[UUI-13]'s metrics are computed, paint is authored from a principle into a load-bearing requirement.

No options: this is a test obligation, not a design choice. A pack theme that can reach the editor's chrome tokens is a defect with a wide blast radius, and it is cheap to assert and expensive to discover late.

EW-9 A 24 px minimum target assumes an input device that is stated but not enforced

Sheet 8 proposes min_target: 24 against touch's 44 and controller's 0, on the strength of [NMTE-S2]'s ruling that a mouse and physical keyboard are strongly recommended. But [CEUI-S2] deliberately kept Branch K's input-mode warning alive, keyed off keyboard-and-mouse presence, precisely because an author can arrive without one — the iPad case Branch K itself called out.

A — 24 px, warn on non-kbm input, accept the hit rate. B — 24 px, and grow to 44 when the input-mode warning would fire. C — 32 px everywhere as a compromise.

Recommendation: A. B is a second responsive state for the editor by another name, and [CEUI-5] spent real cost to eliminate those. C pays for the touch case in the keyboard case's density without actually reaching a touch-safe target. Keyboard reachability of every essential action is a separate obligation and CEUI-40 still owns it — that is the accessibility answer here, not target size.

EW-10 The editor's entry precondition is ratified and unbuilt

[CEUI-S13] makes the editor main-menu-only, which is only safe because the main menu has no active pack. [CSA-28] clause (f) ruled exactly that — quit-to-shell deactivates — but it is not built. DataManager.deactivate_campaign_package() exists and has no production caller; MainMenu.gd reads the installed-pack registry to enable New Game and never touches the active package. So today the main menu is reached with content still loaded.

Nothing currently depends on it, which is why it has gone unnoticed. The editor is the first thing that would — it activates its own working copy, and doing so over a still-active player pack is the provenance failure [CEUI-S9] call 1 exists to prevent.

No options: this is a build precondition and a test, not a design question. Give deactivate_campaign_package() its caller on the path back to the shell, and assert at editor entry that no package is active rather than assuming it. An assumption that is true by ruling and false in code is the most expensive kind.

SHEET 8

The proposed editor token column

proposed

A fourth column, not a second scaling system

[CEUI-S1] ruled the editor is a fourth DENSITY_TOKENS column plus its own multiplier through the same assembler, following [UUI-11]'s precedent. It did not fill the column in. These are the values every frame in this album was laid out from — proposed, and the first thing an implementation would need.

ResponsiveLayout.DENSITY_TOKENS["editor"]
Tokentouchcontrollereditor proposedWhy

row_gap8.02.0 2Dense list, separated by rule lines rather than space.
body_font16.014.0 14Matches controller. Below this, 1.4× translated extent stops fitting a field.

min_target44.00.0 24A real pointer target, below the touch minimum. See EW-9.

min_target is the one that needs an owner's eye. Touch is 44 (Material 48dp / Apple HIG 44pt), controller is 0 because there is no pointer. The editor is proposed at 24 — a real pointer target, but well under the touch minimum, justified by [NMTE-S2]'s ruling that a mouse and physical keyboard are a stated assumption. That assumption is stated, not enforced: [CEUI-S2] kept Branch K's input-mode warning alive precisely because an author can arrive on a touch device anyway. A 24 px target is then a hit-rate problem, not a layout problem. See EW-9.

SHEET 9

Provenance

Where the ruled parts come from. AGENT/Docs/registers/campaign_editor_ui_open_questions_2026-08-12.md — Section A (CEUI-1–8) and the owner rulings [CEUI-S1]–[CEUI-S12], walked 2026-08-14. The precedence check those rulings answer is AGENT/Docs/design/ceui_precedence_diff_2026-08-14.md.

Where the numbers come from. Density tokens are read from scripts/autoloads/ResponsiveLayout.gd; the touch and controller columns in Sheet 8 are that file's actual values. The editor column does not exist yet and is proposed here. Where this album and the engine disagree, the engine wins and the album is stale — that has happened once before and the proof set records it as a finding.

What these frames are. Specifications for a walk, not screenshots and not a component library. They are HTML because HTML lays out and measures a dense dock layout quickly — the UI is Godot scenes. Where a frame and a future build disagree, the frame is the target and the difference is work; where a frame and a ruling disagree, the ruling wins.
